Press Releases New solution combines AI recommendations with archival capabilities to help organizations identify cold data and move it to lower-cost storage, all while keeping it accessible to AI and analytics. NEW YORK, NY – September 16, 2026 – CTERA , a leader in intelligent data management, today announced the new CTERA Data Archiving Solution developed to help organizations identify inactive enterprise data and move it out of expensive primary storage to lower-cost storage tiers. The new solution combines CTERA InsightAI Data Service with CTERA Archive, bringing AI-driven recommendations and a governed workflow to a traditionally manual data lifecycle management process. CTERA Data Archiving Solution is part of the company’s flagship CTERA Intelligent Data Platform. CTERA’s bespoke analysis of over 16 petabytes of live production data, captured across 856 file-share discovery scans in enterprise NAS environments across multiple industries, found that just 4.4% of stored capacity consists of data that users and applications regularly access. Across this massive estate, 88.3% of files had not been accessed in more than a year, while less than 10% of stored capacity had been accessed within the previous 90 days. The challenge for IT teams is determining which data can be safely moved to a lower-cost tier without compromising governance, accessibility, or future value. The CTERA Data Archiving Solution helps IT teams determine what data should be archived and how. CTERA InsightAI uses agentic AI to infer what each file contains from its metadata – filename, path, extension, and directory context – and assess its value to the business, combining that understanding with age, type, size, and usage patterns to recommend which data can be archived. With CTERA Archive, organizations can then move those files to a dedicated, isolated archival tier within the same CTERA environment, while maintaining control over retention and access. Archived data can reside on lower-cost storage hardware or cloud services, providing a more economical alternative to keeping inactive information on primary storage. An analysis of 16 petabytes from enterprise file-share discovery scans finds that vast stores of inactive data are driving up cost, widening security exposure, and undermining AI readiness NEW YORK, NY – September 15, 2026 – CTERA , a leader in intelligent data management, today released new research showing that the vast majority of data sitting on enterprise storage is rarely, if ever, used. An analysis of 16 petabytes of live production data across 856 file-share scans in enterprise NAS environments, including regulated industries, found that just 4.4% of stored capacity is actively used. The rest sits inactive, raising costs, widening security exposure, and undermining AI readiness. The research also found: 83.1% of of the total stored capacity is in files that have not been modified in more than one year. 97.5% of individual files had not been modified in more than one year. 88% of individual files had not been accessed in more than one year, indicating the extent of inactivity across enterprise file environments. Only 9.9% of stored data was accessed in any given 90-day period. These findings point to a common yet costly pattern in which organizations use expensive primary storage as a de facto archive. IT professionals have a term for this accumulated inactive data: ROT, short for Redundant, Obsolete, or Trivial data that exists in duplicate or serves no clear business purpose. While cold data on primary storage is not a new challenge, the research highlights how this ROT data consumes storage as it is backed up, protected, and managed, increasing the resources needed to maintain the overall data estate. The security implications are also significant. Inactive data often remains in the same network-accessible environments and under the same permissions as active data, potentially exposing far more information than employees and applications need for day-to-day operations. The research also highlights an emerging AI-readiness challenge.
